los.text: Consult with a patient effectively via telephone or video conferencing (Zoom), maintaining professional communication.
los.html:
Remote consultation
Before: check identity (name, DOB, address), location (in case of emergency), privacy, who else is present, video/audio working
  • During: introduce yourself and role, check consent, signpost more than usual, speak clearly, pause for delays, check understanding often
  • on the phone listen for cues (breathlessness, tone)
Limitations: no examination (video allows some: breathing, rash, gait); lower threshold to bring in for face-to-face review
End: clear plan, safety-netting (what to watch for, who to call), confirm how results will be shared, document "telephone/video consultation"
Unsuitable: very unwell, safeguarding concerns, language/hearing barriers without support, need for examination

los.text: Take a thorough patient history and explain the results of a CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA), in the context of the patient's clinical presentation.
los.html:
History for suspected PE
  • Sudden pleuritic chest pain, breathlessness, haemoptysis, syncope
  • Risk factors: recent surgery or immobility, long travel, cancer, pregnancy/postpartum, oestrogen (pill, HRT), previous VTE, thrombophilia
  • DVT symptoms (calf swelling).
Wells score >4CTPA; ≤4 → D-dimer (then CTPA if positive).
Explaining a positive CTPA
"The scan shows a blood clot in the blood vessels of your lungs, called a pulmonary embolism"
Why it matters: strains the heart and lowers oxygen
Treatment: anticoagulation (DOAC such as apixaban or rivaroxaban, or LMWH), usually at least 3 months; look for a cause
Bleeding risks and what to watch for; avoid NSAIDs
When to seek urgent help; follow-up

los.text: Engage in interactive revision activities to consolidate knowledge of ICM (Introduction to Clinical Medicine) curriculum topics.
los.html:
Core ICM topics to revise
History structure, ICE, communication skills
CVS, respiratory, GI, neuro, MSK examinations and their findings
A–E assessment, BLS/ALS, sepsis, NEWS2
Procedures: venepuncture, cannulation, blood cultures, injections, ECG, ABG, urinalysis, BMI
Prescribing principles, oxygen, inhalers, insulin

Prescribing insulin
Write "units" in full (never "U" or "IU": misread as 0)
Brand and device specified (e.g. "Lantus SoloStar"), type and strength (U100 standard)
Timing relative to meals
Use the insulin prescription chart (with glucose monitoring record)
Types: rapid-acting (aspart, lispro: with meals), short-acting (soluble), intermediate (isophane), long-acting basal (glargine, detemir, degludec), premixed
Regimens: basal–bolus, twice-daily premixed, once-daily basal (type 2)
Never withhold basal insulin in type 1 diabetes (DKA risk)
Sliding scale / VRIII when nil by mouth; hypoglycaemia protocol
Insulin errors are among the most common serious prescribing errors

los.text: Know how to perform a blood glucose reading
los.html:
• Capillary blood glucose: see ICM Year 1 › Emergencies & A–E › LO 12.
    • Wash hands (patient's too)
    • use the side of the fingertip
    • lancet
    • apply the drop to the strip
    • record the result with time and relation to meals
    • treat <4 mmol/L as hypoglycaemia
    • check ketones if glucose >11 in type 1.
